narrative:
The model estimates a 55% chance that you will leave your job, which is just over the threshold for predicting departure. As a result, the company has decided not to offer you the promotion at this time.

Three factors stood out most in the model’s reasoning. First, the number of training programs you attended in the last three years pushed the prediction most strongly toward you staying. You completed seven or more programs, far more than most employees the model expected to remain. Second, your overall career experience of 6–10 years pulled the prediction toward leaving. While this is fairly common, it is less typical among those the model sees as likely to stay, where half have only 1–5 years of total experience. Third, the length of time you have spent in your current role also worked in your favor, again pointing toward staying because 6–10 years here is longer than most stayers.

Taken together, your strong training record and solid tenure with the organization were working to keep you, but your mid-level total experience sent a stronger signal in the other direction. The model therefore concluded you are more likely to leave than to stay.

Your manager should discuss your career goals openly with you. You may want to explore whether additional responsibilities, clearer growth paths, or changes in workload could increase your sense of stability and satisfaction. Understanding these personal factors can help both you and the organization make better decisions going forward. (248 words)
